lead: The echo from a target is extremely weak: a radar may send hundreds of kilowatts and get back a fraction of a picowatt. The radar range equation follows the power from the transmitter, through the spreading beam, off the target, back through space and into the antenna. It ties transmit power, antenna gain, wavelength, target cross section and receiver noise to one number: the greatest range at which the target can be detected. Every radar design starts from this budget.
prereq: You need antenna gain and effective aperture (G = 4πA<sub>e</sub>/λ²) from Antenna fundamentals and radiation, and noise figure from RF circuits and transceivers.

blocks.text: Take a monostatic radar. The transmitter delivers P<sub>t</sub> watts to an antenna of gain G (a ratio, not dB). On the beam axis at range R metres the power density is P<sub>t</sub>G/(4πR²) W/m²: the power spread over a sphere of area 4πR², multiplied by the gain in the beam direction.

The target intercepts power equal to this density times its radar cross section σ (in m²), and reradiates it. σ is defined so that the reradiation can be treated as equal in all directions (see Radar cross section of targets). Spread over a second sphere on the way back, the echo density at the radar is PtGσ/((4π)²R⁴). Two spreadings of R² give the R⁴.
The antenna collects this density over its effective aperture A<sub>e</sub>. With A<sub>e</sub> = Gλ²/(4π) for the same antenna:

blocks.where: P<sub>r</sub> is the received echo power in W; P<sub>t</sub> the peak transmit power in W; G the antenna gain as a ratio; λ the wavelength in m; σ the radar cross section in m²; R the range in m.

blocks.text: In terms of aperture the same result is P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>A<sub>e</sub>²σ/(4πλ²R⁴). G appears squared because it acts twice: once to focus the transmitted beam and once to capture the echo.

The receiver adds its own noise. Referred to the input, the noise power in the receiver bandwidth B is kT<sub>0</sub>BF, where k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K, T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K and F is the noise figure as a ratio. That is the noise floor, not yet a detection. To declare a target with the wanted probabilities of detection and false alarm, the echo must exceed the noise by a required signal-to-noise ratio (S/N)<sub>min</sub>, typically 10 to 13 dB for one pulse:

Smin = kT0BF·(S/N)min
Here Smin is the minimum detectable signal in W; B is the receiver noise bandwidth in Hz, about 1/τ for a pulse of width τ; F and (S/N)min are ratios.
Losses in the waveguide, duplexer, radome and signal processing are gathered into a system loss L, a ratio greater than 1, which divides the echo: the useful power is P<sub>r</sub>/L.

A radar rarely decides from one pulse. Integrating n pulses raises the signal-to-noise ratio, so the (S/N)<sub>min</sub> needed per pulse falls. Coherent integration (adding the pulses with their phases lined up) gains exactly n. Noncoherent integration (adding after the detector) gains less than n, close to √n when each pulse is weak. In the equations below, (S/N)<sub>min</sub> is the single-pulse value; with integration, divide it by the integration gain.

sections.h3: Maximum range and the fourth-root law

blocks.text: Set P<sub>r</sub>/L = S<sub>min</sub> and solve for R:

Rmax = [PtG²λ²σ / ((4π)³SminL)]1/4
Here Rmax is in metres when every other quantity is in SI units; with apertures, Rmax = [PtAe²σ/(4πλ²SminL)]1/4.

Use the G form or the A<sub>e</sub> form, never a mixture. The fourth root rules radar design. Doubling the range needs 2⁴ = 16 times the power (12 dB). A target with 100 times the cross section is seen only 100<sup>1/4</sup> = 3.16 times farther. The figure plots the echo power of the worked example against range for two targets.

In decibels the equation becomes a budget: 40 log<sub>10</sub> R<sub>max</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>(dBW) + 2G(dB) + 20 log<sub>10</sub> λ + σ(dBsm) − 33.0 − S<sub>min</sub>(dBW) − L(dB), where 33.0 dB is 10 log<sub>10</sub>(4π)³ = 10 log<sub>10</sub> 1984.4. Each line is easy to check, which is why exam answers lay it out as a table.

A search radar must cover a whole volume, not one target. Not every syllabus covers its search form, which uses the average power and the aperture: the product P<sub>av</sub>A<sub>e</sub> sets how large a volume can be searched in a given time at a given range.

examples.question: A monostatic radar transmits P<sub>t</sub> = 500 kW at 10 GHz with an antenna gain of 30 dB. Its minimum detectable signal is S<sub>min</sub> = 1 × 10⁻¹³ W and the losses are 0 dB. (a) Find R<sub>max</sub> for a target of σ = 1 m². (b) Find the power needed to double this range.
steps: R<sub>max</sub>⁴ = 4.5 × 10⁸ / 1.984 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 2.268 × 10¹⁸ m⁴, so R<sub>max</sub> = 38 806 m = 38.8 km.
Doubling the range multiplies R⁴ by 16, so P<sub>t</sub> = 16 × 500 kW = 8 MW.
examples.answer: R<sub>max</sub> = 38.8 km; doubling it needs 8 MW, 12 dB more power.

examples.question: An S-band surveillance radar works at 3 GHz with P<sub>t</sub> = 1.5 MW, G = 33 dB, receiver bandwidth 1 MHz, noise figure 4 dB, required single-pulse (S/N)<sub>min</sub> = 13 dB and system loss 6 dB. Find S<sub>min</sub>, then R<sub>max</sub> for a 2 m² aircraft. How far does it reach if 10 pulses are integrated coherently?
steps: Coherent integration of 10 pulses lowers the needed S<sub>min</sub> by 10, so R<sub>max</sub> grows by 10<sup>1/4</sup> = 1.778 to 165.7 km.
examples.answer: S<sub>min</sub> = 2.0 × 10⁻¹³ W (−127 dBW); R<sub>max</sub> = 93.2 km on one pulse and 165.7 km with 10 pulses integrated coherently.

traps: Taking the noise floor kT<sub>0</sub>BF as the minimum detectable signal. Detection needs the floor times (S/N)<sub>min</sub>; leaving it out makes R<sub>max</sub> too large by (S/N)<sub>min</sub><sup>1/4</sup>, a factor of 2.1 for 13 dB.
Forgetting that G is squared. A 3 dB gain error becomes 6 dB in the echo.
Doubling range with doubled power. It takes 16 times the power, 12 dB more.
Putting F or G in dB into a ratio formula. 10 dB means a ratio of 10, and 30 dB a ratio of 1000.
Mixing units: λ in cm or R in km in a formula written for metres.

quiz.q: Write the radar range equation for the received power of a monostatic radar and define each symbol.
quiz.a: P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>G²λ²σ/((4π)³R⁴): P<sub>t</sub> transmit power in W, G antenna gain (ratio), λ wavelength in m, σ radar cross section in m², R range in m, P<sub>r</sub> echo power in W.

quiz.q: Why does a hundredfold increase in σ raise R<sub>max</sub> only 3.16 times?
quiz.a: R<sub>max</sub> is proportional to σ<sup>1/4</sup>, and 100<sup>1/4</sup> = 3.16.

quiz.q: A radar has R<sub>max</sub> = 20 km. By what factor must P<sub>t</sub> increase to reach 40 km?
quiz.a: R<sub>max</sub>⁴ is proportional to P<sub>t</sub>. Doubling R multiplies R⁴ by 16, so P<sub>t</sub> must rise 16 times (12 dB).

quiz.q: With P<sub>t</sub>, G, σ and S<sub>min</sub> fixed, the frequency is raised from 3 GHz to 12 GHz. Find the new R<sub>max</sub> as a fraction of the old. Would the answer change if the antenna size were kept fixed instead of the gain?
quiz.a: With G fixed, R<sub>max</sub> ∝ λ<sup>1/2</sup>; λ falls to 1/4, so R<sub>max</sub> falls to (1/4)<sup>1/2</sup> = 1/2. With A<sub>e</sub> fixed, R<sub>max</sub> ∝ λ<sup>−1/2</sup>, so it doubles: the same dish has 16 times the gain at 12 GHz.

quiz.q: A receiver has F = 10 dB and B = 1 MHz at T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K, and detection needs 13 dB of S/N. Find the noise floor and S<sub>min</sub>.
Compare coherent and noncoherent integration of n pulses.
quiz.a: Coherent integration adds the pulses before the detector with their phases aligned and raises S/N exactly n times. Noncoherent integration adds after the detector and gains less, near √n for weak pulses; it needs no phase-stable transmitter.

quiz.q: A target at 40 km returns echo power P<sub>r</sub>. If its cross section falls to 1/16, at what range does it return the same P<sub>r</sub>?
quiz.a: P<sub>r</sub> ∝ σ/R⁴, so R⁴ ∝ σ for a fixed P<sub>r</sub>. R falls by (1/16)<sup>1/4</sup> = 1/2, to 20 km.

beyond: Real range predictions add atmospheric loss, the multipath lobes of the ground reflection and a fluctuating target, and quote the range at which detection probability reaches, say, 90 %. Modern radars use many solid-state modules and digital beamforming, but the same fourth-root budget still decides the design. Search for "Blake chart" (a printed range calculation sheet), the search radar equation and detectability factor to go further.

figure.caption: Echo power of the first worked example (500 kW, 30 dB, 10 GHz) falls 40 dB for every tenfold increase in range. It meets the −130 dBW minimum detectable signal at 38.8 km for 1 m²; a target 100 times larger reaches only 122.7 km, 3.16 times farther.

spec.aria: Log graph of echo power in dBW against range from 10 to 200 km. Two straight falling lines, for cross sections of 1 and 100 square metres, cross a dashed line at minus 130 dBW at 38.8 km and 122.7 km.
